<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

arXiv:2608.00894v4 [cs.AR] 18 Nov 2026</div>
</div><div class="ltx_page_content">
<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line ltx_leqno">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:120%;">Ruijie Gao<sup id="id1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup>, Jirong Yang<sup id="id1.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">†</span></sup>,
Mengtian Hong<sup id="id1.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">‡</span></sup>, Youyou Lu<sup id="id1.4" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup>, Barry Lyu<sup id="id1.5" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup>,
Haoran Jin<sup id="id1.6" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup>, and Nathan Bleier<sup id="id1.7" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup></span>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_affiliation_institution"><sup id="id2.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup>University of Michigan  <sup id="id2.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">†</span></sup>The University of Texas at Austin  <sup id="id2.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">‡</span></sup>University of Glasgow</span>, <span id="id3" class="ltx_text ltx_affiliation_institution"><sup id="id3.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup>{ruijieg,yoyolu,barrylyu,allenjin,nbleier}@umich.edu  <sup id="id3.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">†</span></sup>polarisyjr@utexas.edu  <sup id="id3.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">‡</span></sup>2960081H@student.gla.ac.uk</span>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Emerging accelerators rarely ship with mature compiler backends, so recent work
asks LLM agents to write native kernels directly from ISA documentation and
simulator feedback. On two such accelerators, we find that this direct workflow
returns a correct kernel on only 17 of 38 workload instances, and that most of
its inference budget is spent re-deriving machine semantics and repairing
illegal code rather than optimizing the workload.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">We present <span id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span>, which consists of two parts. Contour-Explore
replaces native-code generation with search over
a mapping surface: a typed set of scheduling knobs and their legal domains,
generated automatically from the accelerator’s ISA description and the workload
graph. A compiler-owned resolver completes partial assignments into legal plans
and emits native code, so every evaluated candidate is verified against the
compiler’s default. Kernel writing becomes knob assignment, and kernel
optimization becomes design-space exploration that any policy can drive through
the same intent interface, including hill climbing,
evolutionary search, and LLM agents. Compared with KernelCraft, a
state-of-the-art agentic kernel generator, an LLM agent through Contour-Explore
returns a verified kernel on every Gemmini and PLENA instance, produces
<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.86\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.86</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.86\times</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.13\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.13</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.13\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster kernels on the instances where both
succeed, and uses 26.3% and 83.4% fewer tokens per verified kernel.
KernelCraft returns a correct kernel on only 60% of the Gemmini
instances and 5 of the 18 PLENA instances. The agent’s kernels are also
<math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.17\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.17</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.17\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than those from the expert-written tiling heuristics in
Gemmini’s software library and <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.46\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.46</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.46\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than those from PLENA’s
compiler, and
AccelOpt finds <math id="abstract1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.50\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.50</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.50\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster kernels on Gemmini and <math id="abstract1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.20\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.20</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.20\times</annotation></semantics></math>
faster kernels on four PLENA attention instances when it searches through
Contour-Explore instead of editing kernel programs.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p">A generated surface is bounded by its vocabulary. The second component—Contour-Ext—lifts this bound: when
search stalls, an LLM agent reads the stalled program, hardware facts, and
search history, then extends the backend itself by implementing a new knob and
its lowering. Contour-Ext accepts the extension only if the
default path is byte-identical, every new value is numerically correct and
changes the program, and the enlarged surface yields a measured gain.
On VTA, Contour-Ext extends the AutoTVM surface of TVM, and AutoTVM’s
XGBTuner then finds <math id="abstract1.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.14\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.14</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.14\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster kernels; on PLENA, the extended
surface makes the kernels found by hill climbing <math id="abstract1.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.20\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.20</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.20\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Programmable tensor accelerators often expose target-specific
instruction set architectures, explicitly managed on-chip
memories, and specialized data-movement and control mechanisms
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moreau et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Genc et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jouppi et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.
Supporting such a target requires a tensor compiler backend to lower tensor
operations to these interfaces, including instruction selection, memory
placement, state configuration, and legal instruction sequencing
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ikarashi et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. However, most proposed tensor
accelerators lack reusable tensor compiler backends for generating
implementations beyond supported kernels or templates, and rapid hardware
iteration makes separately engineered backends difficult to maintain
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ikarashi et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
When a reusable backend is unavailable, developers
often fall back on manually written low-level kernels or target-specific
compilation templates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nie et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work has explored large language model (LLM)-based kernel generation
and optimization across GPUs and specialized tensor
accelerators <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
These systems construct and revise kernel programs, guided by compilation,
correctness tests, and performance feedback
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nie et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sereda et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
For example, KernelCraft generates and repairs ISA-level kernels from
machine specifications, using compilation, execution, and correctness
feedback <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nie et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and AccelOpt starts from a correct
kernel and improves performance using beam search, profiling feedback, and
optimization memory distilled from slow–fast kernel pairs
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. We refer to workflows in which agents generate or
revise complete kernel programs as <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">program-level agentic generation</em>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.00894v4/two_knowledge.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:462/141;" width="462" height="141"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1. </span>Kernel generation combines reusable machine-interface knowledge
with workload-dependent mapping decisions.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Across workloads, these workflows involve two classes of information with different
reuse properties (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
Workload-invariant machine knowledge defines the target interface, including
instruction semantics, the memory hierarchy, direct memory access (DMA)
protocols, configuration-state transitions, synchronization, and legality
constraints. Workload-dependent mapping decisions determine how a particular
computation uses that interface, including tiling, scheduling, layout, fusion,
dataflow, and precision. Both are required to produce an executable kernel, but
machine knowledge can be reused across workloads, whereas mapping decisions
generally vary across workload instances.
Without a reusable backend, the agent handles both within the same
per-workload loop, so each invocation spends inference and validation
feedback not only on workload-specific optimization, but also on instruction
legality, configuration-state transitions, data-movement protocols, and
synchronization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Recent advances make this coupling optional. TensorLift recovers executable
tensor-level machine semantics from RTL
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and represents them in the Tensor Accelerator
ISA Definition Language (TAIDL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, from which a
compiler backend can be generated automatically <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Workload-invariant machine knowledge can therefore be compiled once and
reused across agent invocations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.00894v4/per_workload_agentic_loop.svg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/153;" width="476" height="153"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2. </span>Compiler-mediated agentic kernel generation compiles machine
semantics once while searching workload-dependent mappings per
workload, and extends the mapping surface with a validated knob when
search stalls.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">A generated backend takes over machine-specific code generation. Two
problems remain. First, search agents need explicit control over mapping
decisions: where a compiler resolves implicit mapping choices,
program-level workflows treat that completion as a black box and lack
a shared contract for submitting partial mapping decisions and inspecting
their resolution.
Second, the compiler defines which mapping decisions an agent can
express, and this set bounds every search policy: a mapping that no
published decision expresses cannot be reached, whereas a program-level
agent can write it directly. We address the first problem by separating
mapping search from compiler-owned completion and native code generation,
and the second by letting an agent extend the compiler when search stalls
(Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We present <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span>, an agentic framework in which search agents
choose mapping decisions and the compiler generates the kernel.
<span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span> consists of two parts: Contour-Explore searches a mapping
surface, and Contour-Ext extends it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Contour-Explore derives a workload-conditioned mapping surface from
formal, RTL-lifted machine semantics and publishes each mapping decision as
a typed knob with its legal values. The agent submits a mapping intent:
required or preferred knob values, with other decisions left to the
compiler. For example, it may select an algorithm, prefer a tile size, and
leave loop organization unspecified. A symbolic resolver completes a legal
mapping for the backend to lower to native code; completing an empty
intent yields a verified default kernel, <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span>, which initializes
search. During search, feedback reports the realized mapping values,
correctness, and performance to guide the agent’s next mapping hypothesis.
A <em id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">search agent</em>, the component that proposes mapping intents,
can implement an LLM-based policy or a conventional search policy, such as
hill climbing, evolutionary search, or random sampling; all policies
share the same mapping surface, symbolic completion, code generation, and
candidate-validation path.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Contour-Ext extends the mapping surface when search in Contour-Explore
stalls. An LLM-based <em id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">extension agent</em> analyzes the stalled kernel and
the search history, then implements a new knob and its lowering in the
compiler. Contour-Ext keeps the knob only if it passes correctness and
effectiveness checks, after which Contour-Explore republishes the surface and
search continues. The agent’s ability to write low-level code is thereby
applied to the compiler instead of to a single kernel: an accepted knob is
checked once and then remains available to later workloads and to every
search policy. Contour-Ext requires only a knob registry, a lowering, legality
checks, and an evaluator from its host compiler, so it also applies to
existing compilers such as TVM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2018a</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">This paper makes the following contributions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We characterize how program-level agentic generation repeatedly
reconstructs workload-invariant machine semantics on accelerators without
a reusable kernel-generation backend: when we replicate KernelCraft
on PLENA, repairing programs and reasoning about machine semantics take
<math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.1\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.1\times</annotation></semantics></math> the completion tokens spent on optimizing correct programs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design Contour-Explore, a workload-conditioned mapping-search
interface that publishes typed decisions derived from the hardware
specification and the workload. It supports partial intents with
required, preferred, and automatic decisions, completes them into legal
plans, and reports the realized mapping values as feedback to guide
subsequent search.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design Contour-Ext, which extends the mapping surface when
search stalls with knobs that pass correctness and effectiveness checks.
On 16 VTA instances, Contour-Ext extends the AutoTVM surface of TVM, and
AutoTVM’s XGBTuner finds <math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.14\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.14</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.14\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster kernels on the extended
surface than on the original one. On 18 PLENA instances, the extended
surface makes the kernels found by hill climbing <math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.20\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.20</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.20\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate Contour-Explore against KernelCraft, AccelOpt, and
the software shipped with each accelerator: the tiled matrix-multiply
routine in Gemmini’s official software library and the compiler of PLENA.
An LLM agent searching through
Contour-Explore returns a correct kernel on every Gemmini and PLENA
instance, whereas KernelCraft fails on 21 of the 38; where both succeed,
the agent’s kernels are faster and cost fewer tokens. The agent’s
kernels are also <math id="S1.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.17\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.17</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.17\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than the Gemmini library routine and
<math id="S1.I1.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.46\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.46</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.46\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than those of the PLENA compiler. AccelOpt also finds
faster kernels when it searches through Contour-Explore than when it edits
kernel programs.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1. </span>Emerging Accelerator Architectures</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study three representative accelerator platforms: Gemmini
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Genc et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, an established state-of-the-art tensor-accelerator
generator; PLENA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, a recently introduced open-source
research accelerator for long-context agentic LLM inference; and VTA
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moreau et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, an open-source deep-learning accelerator. All
three expose
target-specific instructions and explicitly managed on-chip memories, so
mapping a tensor computation requires coordinating its computational
decomposition with data placement and movement.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Gemmini.</span>
Gemmini is an open-source, full-stack DNN accelerator generator integrated with
RISC-V systems. Its central compute structure is a configurable spatial array
whose processing elements perform
multiply–accumulate operations using weight- or output-stationary dataflow.
The array reads operands from a banked, explicitly managed scratchpad and
writes partial and final results to a higher-precision accumulator. A Gemmini
mapping therefore determines how matrices are tiled, staged through the
scratchpad, accumulated, and executed under the selected dataflow.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PLENA.</span>
PLENA is designed for long-context agentic LLM inference and organizes its ISA
around Matrix, Vector, Scalar, HBM, and Control instruction classes. Its Matrix
Unit uses an output-stationary flattened systolic array: operands stream along
a long reduction dimension while sub-arrays retain partial sums, which are
combined by a cross-array reduction.
PLENA separates its on-chip storage into a Vector SRAM for activations and
vector intermediates and a Matrix SRAM for weights and KV tensors. The latter
supports transposed and non-transposed reads without explicitly rearranging
the stored data, directly supporting computations such as <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="QK^{\mathsf{T}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>𝖳</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">QK^{\mathsf{T}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The Vector Unit complements matrix multiplication with elementwise,
reduction, and nonlinear operations needed by normalization and softmax.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">PLENA composes these capabilities at tile granularity. Independent HBM
prefetch paths can fill the Matrix and Vector SRAMs while other units execute,
and fine-grained scheduling can interleave matrix multiplication, vector
reduction, scalar control, and data movement within a fused attention
pipeline. The architecture also supports mixed-precision MX formats across
its storage and compute paths. Its programmable mapping surface consequently
includes matrix and vector tiling, cross-array reduction, tensor orientation,
SRAM placement and residency, prefetching and buffering, numerical precision,
fusion, and overlap across execution units. Together, these are hardware-level mapping
decisions that the compilation approaches below must ultimately realize.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">VTA.</span>
The Versatile Tensor Accelerator (VTA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moreau et al., 2019</a>)</cite> is the
open-source deep-learning accelerator of the TVM compiler
stack <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2018a</a>)</cite>. Its GEMM core multiplies int8 tiles held in
explicitly managed on-chip buffers and accumulates in int32. Its load,
compute, and store modules run concurrently and synchronize through
dependency queues, so data movement can overlap computation. TVM generates
VTA code from a schedule, which fixes the tiling, loop order, and on-chip
buffer placement of a tensor operator; its VTA backend maps the scheduled
loops to VTA load, GEMM, ALU, and store instructions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2. </span>Machine Semantics and Generated Backends</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use <em id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">compiler backend</em> to mean the target-specific component
that translates a tensor computation graph into accelerator assembly. Prior
work provides the machine semantics that a backend needs in machine-readable
form. The Tensor Accelerator ISA Definition Language (TAIDL) describes
accelerator state, instruction semantics, and legality constraints using
tensor operations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. TensorLift generates TAIDL from
RTL: it lifts bit-accurate architectural-state updates into tensor-level
descriptions of computation, data movement, and control, and validates them
against the low-level model with SMT proofs and simulation
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. A compiler backend can then be generated
from the TAIDL specification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2026</a>)</cite>; on seven Gemmini
workloads, TensorLift with such a backend achieves a <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.014\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.014</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.014\times</annotation></semantics></math>
geometric-mean speedup over the official handwritten kernels
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These systems provide reusable machine semantics and native code generation,
but do not expose workload-level mapping decisions to an external search
policy or accept partially specified mapping intents. <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span> introduces
a mapping-search interface that publishes the decisions available for each
workload and accepts required, preferred, and automatic choices.
Its symbolic resolver completes partial intents into legal plans
and reports their realized mapping values as feedback. The mapping surface,
intent interface, resolver, and feedback-directed search workflow are
introduced by this work.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">

<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3. </span>Program-Level Agentic Generation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">KernelCraft studies a different response to the absence of a reusable
backend: a tool-using LLM agent directly generates and repairs a close-to-metal
kernel for each workload <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nie et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Each task supplies a
concrete workload instance, the target ISA and hardware
documentation, and memory-layout information. A platform-specific execution
harness gives the agent access to the target compiler, simulator, correctness
oracle, and documentation retrieval. Together, these inputs and services form
the agent’s context. The required output is an ISA-level program that
explicitly realizes both the computation and its use of the target machine.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Generation proceeds as a multi-turn diagnosis-and-repair loop. In each
iteration, the agent produces a candidate assembly program, compiles and
executes it, and receives syntax diagnostics, functional differences, and
execution latency. When additional machine information is needed, the agent
queries the supplied ISA and hardware documentation through
<span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grep_docs</span>. It uses this feedback first to repair correctness and then
to optimize performance, repeating the loop until its interaction budget is
exhausted.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Because the generated artifact is already close to the target ISA, the agent
is responsible for more than workload mapping. Within the same program, it
must select instructions, calculate addresses, place values in the memory
hierarchy, schedule data movement and computation, manage configuration state,
and expose parallelism. KernelCraft shows that frontier agents can sometimes
produce correct, performance-competitive kernels for unfamiliar accelerators.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Program-level agents can also optimize an existing kernel. AccelOpt
organizes this process around three agents: a planner, executor, and
summarizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. In its workflow, the planner
proposes optimizations using profiling
feedback and accumulated experience; the executor implements these plans as
kernel programs; and the summarizer distills reusable optimization insights
from slow–fast kernel pairs for subsequent exploration. In its Trainium
implementation, the agents receive hardware constraints and NKI programming
guidance through platform-specific prompts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4. </span>Motivation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">KernelCraft’s program-level generation workflow treats each workload task in isolation.
Although the target ISA, memory organization, and instruction semantics remain
unchanged across tasks, the workflow does not carry the machine-specific
knowledge recovered for one task into the next. Consequently, the target
details required for native-code generation remain part of every per-workload
interaction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">When we replicate KernelCraft’s experiments on PLENA with its benchmark
workloads, including GEMM, GEMV, normalization, softmax, FFN, and attention,
and classify each model turn by tool verdict and by content,
most completion tokens go to repairing programs and to reasoning about
<em id="S2.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">machine semantics</em>: instruction semantics, operand conventions, memory
layout, precision formats, legality, and timing. These two uses take
<math id="S2.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.1\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.1\times</annotation></semantics></math> the completion tokens and <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.8\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.8</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.8\times</annotation></semantics></math> the reasoning tokens spent
on optimizing correct programs (Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.2. Machine Semantics and Generated Backends ‣ 2. Preliminaries ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Every run
spends 9.7–50.9% of its completion tokens on this workload-invariant
knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This observation motivates our compiler-mediated agentic design: a reusable
compiler captures target-invariant code-generation knowledge and
generates every candidate from the validated machine semantics, so that
candidates are legal by construction and the agent can spend its tokens on
workload-specific mapping decisions instead of program repair.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Design</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span> consists of two parts (Figure <a href="#acmlabel1" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3. Design ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
<span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contour-Explore</span> connects a search agent to a reusable compiler through a
workload-specific mapping interface. The agent chooses how to map a tensor
computation; the compiler completes these choices and generates target code.
An independent evaluator checks the output and measures performance. A
controller returns these results to the agent and retains the fastest verified
candidate. The same interface supports neural and conventional search policies.
<span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contour-Ext</span> extends this interface when search stalls. An extension
agent implements a new knob and its lowering in the compiler, and Contour-Ext
keeps the new knob only if it passes correctness and effectiveness
checks.
Sections <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. Constructing the Mapping Surface ‣ 3. Design ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>–<a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4. Code Generation and Candidate Validation ‣ 3. Design ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a> describe
Contour-Explore, and Section <a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5. Extending the Mapping Surface ‣ 3. Design ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a> describes Contour-Ext.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.00894v4/overview.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/205;" width="476" height="205" aria-label="Block diagram. In Contour-Explore, a surface generator reads the
workload and target and publishes a surface and Candidate-0 to search.
Search sends intents to the resolver, which passes plans to the schedule
layer and code generation; the evaluator returns latency and numerics.
When search stalls, Contour-Ext diagnoses, proposes a knob, implements a patch,
and validates it; an accepted patch produces the next surface."><p>Block diagram. In Contour-Explore, a surface generator reads the
workload and target and publishes a surface and Candidate-0 to search.
Search sends intents to the resolver, which passes plans to the schedule
layer and code generation; the evaluator returns latency and numerics.
When search stalls, Contour-Ext diagnoses, proposes a knob, implements a patch,
and validates it; an accepted patch produces the next surface.</p></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3. </span><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span> overview: Contour-Explore searches the published
mapping surface, and Contour-Ext extends it when search stalls.<span id="acmlabel1" class="ltx_acm_description ltx_centering ltx_nodisplay">Block diagram. In Contour-Explore, a surface generator reads the
workload and target and publishes a surface and Candidate-0 to search.
Search sends intents to the resolver, which passes plans to the schedule
layer and code generation; the evaluator returns latency and numerics.
When search stalls, Contour-Ext diagnoses, proposes a knob, implements a patch,
and validates it; an accepted patch produces the next surface.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Mapping search with explicit preference completion</figcaption>
<table id="alg1.6" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">

            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l39.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">39:</span></span>
            
            
          <span id="alg1.l39.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">   </span><span id="alg1.l39.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">end</span><span id="alg1.l39.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="alg1.l39.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l40" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l40.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">40:</span></span>
            
            
          <span id="alg1.l40.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">   Construct plan sections and schedule DAG; reject cycles
</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l41" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l41.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">41:</span></span>
            
            
          <span id="alg1.l41.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">   </span><span id="alg1.l41.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">return</span><span id="alg1.l41.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> plan with realized decisions and resolution records
</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l42" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l42.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">42:</span></span>
            
            
          <span id="alg1.l42.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">end</span><span id="alg1.l42.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="alg1.l42.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">function</span>
</div>
</div>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>Constructing the Mapping Surface</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The input is a tensor computation in the high-level optimizer (HLO)
intermediate representation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenXLA, 0000</a>)</cite> and a target described by TAIDL. A
<em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">workload contract</em> fixes the computation, input data, target,
execution boundary, and numerical acceptance policy for every candidate.
Within this contract, a <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS1.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="12.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-1.77px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 12.45 12.45" width="12.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,12.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(6.23,0) translate(0,6.23)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#1766B2;" fill="#1766B2"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 6.23 0 C 6.23 3.44 3.44 6.23 0 6.23 C -3.44 6.23 -6.23 3.44 -6.23 0 C -6.23 -3.44 -3.44 -6.23 0 -6.23 C 3.44 -6.23 6.23 -3.44 6.23 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.98 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.56em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="7.96"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">1</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text"><em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#BEDBFA;">mapping surface</em></span> lists the decisions that search
may change, such as tiling, operand residency, or execution overlap. Each
decision, or <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">knob</em>, has a type and a finite domain of supported values.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The surface generator constructs a workload-specific mapping surface using a TAIDL
hardware description and a shared mapping layer. TAIDL specifies architectural
state, storage capacities, instruction semantics, and legality constraints.
The shared mapping layer defines the knob vocabulary and default policies,
which are compiler design choices reused across accelerators. For each
workload, the surface generator uses the hardware description and these shared policies
to <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#BEDBFA;">derive the available knob values</span>, and the resolver
checks their joint legality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The shared mapping layer defines each knob category with four parts:
a derivation rule that creates knob instances and candidate domains from the
workload graph and TAIDL facts, a default policy, a legality predicate for
its values, and a plan field that lowering reads. We call these four parts a
<em id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">knob definition</em>. A <em id="S3.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">compiler version</em> is the compiler together
with its registered knob definitions. The surface generator publishes one
surface for each compiler version. Contour-Ext (Section <a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5. Extending the Mapping Surface ‣ 3. Design ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>)
registers new knob definitions through the same interface, so added knobs
and built-in knobs use the same derivation, publication, and completion
steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">On PLENA, the surface generator first selects the knob categories applicable to the
operator family. The eight categories cover algorithm, matrix and vector
decomposition, placement, memory pipeline, execution pipeline, precision, and
loop structure. For each applicable knob, it tests each supported value by
requiring that value and completing the remaining decisions with the default
policies. It retains values whose completion passes the constraints and omits
knobs with only one retained value. Those fixed choices remain compiler-owned.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">These per-knob tests do not make the domains independently combinable. The
resolver checks joint constraints again when it completes an intent. For
example, the attention algorithm determines whether scores are materialized;
that choice changes SRAM demand and the legal block sizes. A conditional
surface therefore publishes individual domains without enumerating their
cross-product. Gemmini instead uses a finite catalog of complete mappings
that pass the workload’s shape, capacity, and scheduling checks. Both forms
expose legal choices without exposing physical instructions or addresses.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>Completing Mapping Intents</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">intent</em> assigns values to exposed knobs. <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span> supports
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS2.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="12.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-1.77px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 12.45 12.45" width="12.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,12.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(6.23,0) translate(0,6.23)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#946000;" fill="#946000"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 6.23 0 C 6.23 3.44 3.44 6.23 0 6.23 C -3.44 6.23 -6.23 3.44 -6.23 0 C -6.23 -3.44 -3.44 -6.23 0 -6.23 C 3.44 -6.23 6.23 -3.44 6.23 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.98 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.56em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="7.96"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS2.p1.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">2</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text"><em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#FFE09B;">hard</em></span> assignments that must hold and
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS2.p1.pic2" class="ltx_picture" height="12.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-1.77px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 12.45 12.45" width="12.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,12.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(6.23,0) translate(0,6.23)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#007357;" fill="#007357"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 6.23 0 C 6.23 3.44 3.44 6.23 0 6.23 C -3.44 6.23 -6.23 3.44 -6.23 0 C -6.23 -3.44 -3.44 -6.23 0 -6.23 C 3.44 -6.23 6.23 -3.44 6.23 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.98 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.56em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="7.96"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS2.p1.pic2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">3</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text"><em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.4.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#A9E2CB;">preferred</em></span> assignments that may be relaxed.
The resolver rejects unknown knobs and values outside the published domains,
and fills automatic or omitted choices using shared default policies.
Gemmini selects a complete catalog mapping and treats all selected values
as hard assignments; PLENA also supports partial intents with preferences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For PLENA, completion first applies all <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#FFE09B;">hard assignments</span> together. The
resolver fills the remaining choices with the shared default policies and
checks shape, capacity, reduction, output-coverage, and dependency constraints.
If this completion fails, it <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#FFE09B;">rejects the intent</span>. It then processes preferences
in a <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#A9E2CB;">fixed order</span>: category order followed by knob-name order. For each
preference, it adds the requested assignment to the accepted assignments and
attempts completion again. A successful check <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#A9E2CB;">retains the assignment</span>; a
failure <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#A9E2CB;">drops it</span> and records the requested value, realized value, and reason.
Preferences are incorporated incrementally in a fixed order, retaining each
choice only when its completion remains legal alongside previously accepted
assignments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Mapping completion produces a <em id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">resolved plan</em>: a complete legal mapping with eight
semantic sections for the computation graph, matrix and vector decomposition,
placement, memory, precision, pipeline, and loops. It also constructs an
engine-schedule directed acyclic graph (DAG) specifying operations and
dependencies, rejecting cyclic schedules. Internal resolution records identify
defaulted choices and honored or relaxed preferences. The resolved decisions
guide subsequent lowering of the tensor computation to target code.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span>Feedback-Directed Search</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Search begins by completing the empty intent. The resulting default plan,
<span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span>, uses the shared default policies under the target and
workload constraints. It requires no model inference. The controller compiles,
executes, and verifies this plan before using it as the initial
<em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">incumbent</em>, the fastest verified candidate so far. The agent receives
the workload, surface, default decisions and performance, and remaining
evaluation budget. PLENA additionally reports a bottleneck profile containing
engine activity, HBM traffic, and SRAM occupancy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Gemmini: selecting a legal point.</span>
The agent sees the catalog’s mapping decisions, with performance hidden for
untried mappings. It submits one complete mapping per evaluation. The
controller rejects duplicate submissions and returns verification, measured
cycles, and structural properties for each newly evaluated mapping. The agent
can then refine a tile choice or explore different buffering and store
schedules. Only candidates evaluated within the run enter final selection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PLENA: proposing a region.</span>
A <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS3.p3.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="12.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-1.77px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 12.45 12.45" width="12.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,12.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(6.23,0) translate(0,6.23)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#B32661;" fill="#B32661"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 6.23 0 C 6.23 3.44 3.44 6.23 0 6.23 C -3.44 6.23 -6.23 3.44 -6.23 0 C -6.23 -3.44 -3.44 -6.23 0 -6.23 C 3.44 -6.23 6.23 -3.44 6.23 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.98 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.56em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="7.96"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS3.p3.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">4</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text"><em id="S3.SS3.p3.1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#F5BDD4;">search region</em></span> describes how the controller should generate candidate
intents. Hard assignments remain fixed; preferred assignments guide sampling;
explicitly automatic knobs are left to compiler completion. Other unassigned
knobs remain available for sampling. Each region includes at least one
<em id="S3.SS3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">diversity axis</em>, identifying a knob along which alternative plans are
desired, and leaves at least two knobs free of hard assignments. It may also
name an evaluated plan as a center and specify an initial radius in changed
decisions. Diversity guides sampling and selection without adding legality
constraints.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The controller constructs a center using preferred values, then the named
plan’s remaining values, or domain midpoints when no plan is named. Explicitly
automatic knobs remain omitted from <span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#F5BDD4;">candidate intents</span>. Without a named
plan, the controller <span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#F5BDD4;">samples</span> up to 256 assignments: preferred knobs take
their requested values with probability 0.75 and otherwise draw uniformly;
other free knobs draw uniformly. With a named plan, sampling changes one to
the radius’s number of knobs, prioritizing diversity axes. Each sampled
assignment becomes a candidate intent whose sampled values are preferences
and whose hard assignments are preserved from the region.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The controller <span id="S3.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#F5BDD4;">removes rejected intents</span> and plans that duplicate either
previous evaluations or other plans in the pool. Deduplication uses the eight
semantic sections. If a neighborhood supplies fewer than two fresh plans, it
expands the radius up to eight; a pool still smaller than two is rejected.
It <span id="S3.SS3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#F5BDD4;">filters the worst quarter</span> by estimated static cost, preserving the center
and at least two plans. This estimate filters candidates rather than choosing
the measured winner.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#F5BDD4;">Two plans enter evaluation</span>. The first is the center when available; otherwise,
it is the plan most distant from previously evaluated plans. The second
prioritizes a new value on the first diversity axis, then maximizes distance
from the first plan and evaluated plans. Distance is normalized Hamming
distance over the eight semantic sections. Both plans obey the hard
assignments, but their realized preferences can differ after completion.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3. Design ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> combines this target-specific proposal path
with the common search loop. Feedback reports each plan’s identity,
verification, measured performance, and realized decisions relative to the
default. A rejected region instead receives a mapping-level explanation,
such as conflicting hard assignments or exhausted alternatives. The agent can
revise its proposal, but only the controller can update the incumbent.
The controller bounds both proposals and evaluations. Rejected regions consume
requests without consuming evaluations, so repeated rejection cannot prolong
search indefinitely. A new batch requires sufficient remaining evaluation
budget; <span id="S3.SS3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Candidate-0</span> is outside this search budget.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conventional search policies.</span>
Hill climbing, genetic search, and random sampling implement the
<span id="S3.SS3.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Propose</span> step in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3. Design ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> over the published
mapping decisions. Hill climbing explores neighboring assignments, genetic
search mutates and recombines typed intents, and random search samples
assignments from the exposed domains. <span id="S3.SS3.p8.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span> completes these proposals
into legal mappings and generates kernels for verification and measurement.
Measured latency provides the objective value for hill climbing and genetic
selection; random sampling proceeds independently of these values. Across
all policies, the controller retains the fastest verified candidate. Thus,
conventional policies search mapping choices without implementing kernel
generation or legality checks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stall detection.</span>
Search <em id="S3.SS3.p9.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">stalls</em> when the incumbent stops improving: the relative
latency improvement over a window of recent evaluations falls below a
threshold, or the policy can reach no unevaluated program. An exploration
round also ends when an LLM search agent produces no new evaluation for a
fixed number of turns, or when the round’s evaluation budget is spent. The
incumbent at the end of the round is the <em id="S3.SS3.p9.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">stalled plan</em>, <math id="S3.SS3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Contour-Ext (Section <a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5. Extending the Mapping Surface ‣ 3. Design ‣ Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>) starts from <math id="S3.SS3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4. </span>Code Generation and Candidate Validation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Gemmini realization.</span>
<span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span> exposes macro tiling, buffering, store scheduling, and batch-region
choices through a legal mapping catalog. Macro-tile dimensions are multiples
of the primitive tile, bounded by workload dimensions and scratchpad and
accumulator capacities. The selected mapping specifies the choices that the
subsequent schedule transformations must realize; choices with only one
applicable value remain fixed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The existing generated backend <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS4.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="12.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-1.77px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 12.45 12.45" width="12.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,12.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(6.23,0) translate(0,6.23)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#AD480D;" fill="#AD480D"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 6.23 0 C 6.23 3.44 3.44 6.23 0 6.23 C -3.44 6.23 -6.23 3.44 -6.23 0 C -6.23 -3.44 -3.44 -6.23 0 -6.23 C 3.44 -6.23 6.23 -3.44 6.23 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.98 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.56em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="7.96"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS4.p2.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">5</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#FFCBA8;">lowers the HLO computation</span>
to a primitive schedule with concrete transfer and matrix-operation addresses
and sizes. <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span> then applies schedule transformations to implement
accumulator initialization, the selected buffering strategy, and store order.
The schedule parser checks the transformed schedule before code generation.
This additional transformation stage connects the searchable mapping choices
to their executable realization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PLENA realization.</span>
The resolver translates the completed mapping into typed bridge options that
<span id="S3.SS4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span> passes to code generation, making the resolved computation,
placement, data movement, and execution overlap explicit inputs to lowering.
Instruction selection, physical memory management, and synchronization realize
these decisions as <span id="S3.SS4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#FFCBA8;">target code</span>. From the same options,
the resolver derives an engine-schedule DAG for symbolic legality checks and
cost estimation. The mapping interface thus gives search control over the
plan realized by the backend.
A schedule layer reads the plan fields and selects operator
decompositions, placement, tensor storage, and loop nests before instruction
selection. Instruction selection maps abstract tile operations to target
instructions by semantic signatures derived from TAIDL. Lowering either
implements every value in a resolved plan or reports that it cannot; it
does not fall back to another value. On request, lowering tags each
instruction with the schedule-layer step that produced it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Independent validation.</span>
The evaluator <span id="S3.SS4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#FFCBA8;">executes</span> each generated program and
<span id="S3.SS4.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#FFCBA8;">compares</span> its complete output with an independent numerical oracle under the workload contract.
The acceptance policy remains fixed across mapping and precision choices.
The evaluator returns correctness and performance to the controller,
together with structural counters when available. A candidate replaces the incumbent only when it
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS4.p4.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="12.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-1.77px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 12.45 12.45" width="12.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,12.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(6.23,0) translate(0,6.23)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#6D31AE;" fill="#6D31AE"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 6.23 0 C 6.23 3.44 3.44 6.23 0 6.23 C -3.44 6.23 -6.23 3.44 -6.23 0 C -6.23 -3.44 -3.44 -6.23 0 -6.23 C 3.44 -6.23 6.23 -3.44 6.23 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.98 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.56em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="7.96"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS4.p4.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">6</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> <span id="S3.SS4.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#D5BDF2;">passes verification</span> and <span id="S3.SS4.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#D5BDF2;">strictly improves</span> the performance objective. Otherwise,
the previous verified candidate remains the result. The agent cannot change
the acceptance criteria or the final selection rule.
The evaluator identifies each program by a hash of its assembly and
does not execute the same program twice. <span id="S3.SS4.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Contour</span> keeps the hashes of
all programs measured in the run.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div id="alg2.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg2.l3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3:</span></span>
              
              
            <span id="alg2.l3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">while</span><span id="alg2.l3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> the proposal budget permits </span><span id="alg2.l3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">do</span><span id="alg2.l3.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">
</span>
</div>
<div id="alg2.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg2.l4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4:</span></span>
              
              
            <span id="alg2.l4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">   </span><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="alg2.l4.pic1" class="ltx_picture" color="#000000"             <span id="alg2.l17.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">    </span><math id="alg2.l17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathsize="0.800em">p</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathsize="0.800em">∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p^{*}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg2.l17.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> is not faster than </span><math id="alg2.l17.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathsize="0.800em">p</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathsize="0.800em">s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg2.l17.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> by the gain threshold
</span>
</div>
<div id="alg2.l18" class="ltx_listingline">

            <span id="alg2.l18.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">    a new value exceeds the error bound on scaled or
</span>
</div>

</span><math id="alg2.l20.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(C^{\prime},p^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathsize="0.800em">C</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathsize="0.800em">′</mo></msup><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathsize="0.800em">,</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathsize="0.800em">p</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathsize="0.800em">∗</mo></msup><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(C^{\prime},p^{*})</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg2.l20.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">
</span>
</div>
<div id="alg2.l21" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg2.l21.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">21:</span></span>

</span>
</div>
<div id="alg2.l22" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg2.l22.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">22:</span></span>
